video_title: Stephen McLennan: Building the Total Portfolio at Ontario Teachers' $300B Fund
transcript: Stephen, thank you very much for joining me . Thanks for inviting me, Ted. I'm looking forward to the next hour or so and am a big fan of the podcast. I would be happy if you could take me back to an early experience that you can later recall and say influenced your investing. In preparation for this particular session, I tried to reflect on what gave me the investment bug, so to speak. And, to be honest, I'm not sure what it was. It must have been something to do with 80s pop culture, movies and TV shows of that time. However, my first experience in the world of investing was in high school, my senior year . I took a co-op session at one of the local brokerage firms, and it coincided with the first Gulf War. And I think what was amazing, as tragic as these circumstances were for people on the ground, was the connection between what was happening in the real world, in terms of what was happening on CNN, and how that immediately translated into what was happening in the markets. And you could see that reaction in real time. So I guess that was the beginning of how I started thinking about the world of investing. You know, I've done a lot of different things in my career, so I think each of those experiences has probably shaped my thinking about the world and how I think about forming that kind of investment view. What were these experiences like , and how did they shape your views? After graduating from school, I earned a bachelor's degree in business, economics, and finance. And my first job out of school was working for Archer Daniels Midland, a large American agribusiness company, for their Canadian operations. And it was a great job for beginners. It involved buying and selling grain, logistics, and hedging on the Chicago Board of Trade, and it was a really interesting attempt to delve into the world of business. It wasn't necessarily a purely investment role, but the plan was always to go back to school to get an MBA, so I went back to school, and after my MBA I joined Merrill Lynch in their Calgary office. So, speaking to your story, Calgary—it's kind of the energy hub of Canada, the Houston of Canada, if you will, and it's a very capital-intensive sector, so this work required a lot of capital raising, and Merrill was very well- positioned to do that. At that time, there was a lot of activity from American companies coming in and buying up some of the Canadian exploration and production businesses, so I got that experience, which was a fantastic experience, but I really started to shape different parts of the investment world , although not as an investor. For personal reasons, my then- girlfriend, now wife, wanted to move back to Toronto to go back to school and be closer to her family; and so I wanted to use this as an opportunity to think about how and what, what's the next step in my career, or the next stage of my career, and how do I want to position myself to approach the investment process? So, move from the role of an investment banker's agent to the role of an investor, which is more principled, and see this as an opportunity to return to learning. As you can see, teaching is a great environment from a learning perspective, and this lifestyle is truly attractive. The problem is that sometimes it's not exactly the real world, and, you know, the pay may not be as good as it is in the more professional world. So I used that to go back to school, got a degree in mathematical finance here in Toronto, and then joined the teachers as a newbie, a younger person trying to get closer to the investment process. So I joined the credit department, and given my experience, it was a broad mandate at the time. It was 2003. As for the lending business, it was, well, you know, traditional corporate bonds, some private placements. But at that time, credit derivatives were quite a growing business, and that's where I spent most of my time, thinking about how best to use this product or, so to speak, implementing whatever views we thought were appropriate at the time. It was a wonderful experience. I would say that as you know, the global financial crisis (GFC) was actually, its epicenter was a credit event and a credit derivatives event. And so I have a lot of scars on my back from that particular experience, in terms of how you deal with liquidity, counterparties, how you think about risk positioning and all sorts of other things. Some of these locks and responses, portfolio construction if you are a portfolio manager . Eventually, I was promoted to head of the credit team, and it was a great experience, and it was a fantastic team. However, in 2013, the head of our capital markets group was tasked with creating a new program called Natural Resources, which would be a combination of our government goods program, which we use because of its inflationary characteristics, with a desire or aspiration to develop a private natural resources program so that it would really complement these government goods exposures. So it was a great opportunity for me to work with a new group of colleagues, work for a new manager, and really build a business, and try to think through what this portfolio should look like, based both on my experience teaching in the energy field and some aspects of portfolio building. We managed to bring the private part of this program to a certain level, and then, against the backdrop of some other organizational changes, try to optimize the number of programs or places where private investments were made. They moved me and a few colleagues to a renamed group called Infrastructure and Natural Resources. And that really gave me an idea of ​​the infrastructure part of the portfolio. I had day-to-day responsibilities for natural resources, but I got to know the infrastructure team, these assets, and how they impact the overall portfolio. And then, around 2018, when the previous head of capital markets was promoted to CIO , he asked me to come in and help him set up a new group where he thought he would like to have a new team called " All Funds Management," which certainly has some characteristics of what became known as the TPA concept. I'm something of a TPA, but the thoughts for this TFM group were to merge our asset allocation function with our treasury function. So I always try to explain that asset allocation is what you want to buy, and treasury is how you pay for it? And it was a great combination of my public market experience with my private market experience, bringing together those two building blocks. And one of the lessons I've learned throughout my career is that the public and private sectors, even though these two market participants or groups of market participants are sometimes almost of different religions and don't like each other or like to argue and throw stones at each other, are simply instruments for implementing a common policy view or a portfolio view. So this was a great opportunity for me to help the organization build a portfolio to try to deliver on the, um, pension promise. Uh, fast forward a couple of years, and the CIO has resigned . Organizationally, we spent time thinking about what the right structure would be going forward, and we arrived at a model with a dual CIO or co-CIO . I am one of the directors of information technology. We've split the responsibilities between asset allocation, and my colleague Gillian Brown, CIO for Public and Private Investments , is actually responsible for these active programs. Why don't we take a step back and ask you to tell Teachers' story? We were founded in our current format in 1990. The origin story is that in the 1980s, the Teachers' Union and the Province of Ontario, our joint sponsors, started to worry about the long-term sustainability of the plan, so a series of different commissions and studies were conducted, which, um, um, and concluded with the creation of an independent organization called the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan Board. A few key things that were really important in the beginning were, um, independence and first-class management. Another requirement was to make sure we were run like a business and had the management style of a world-class asset management company. The first thing the board did was hire our founding CEO , Claude Lamoureux. And the first thing Claude did, or one of the first things Claude did, was hire our CIO , Bob Bertram. Both Bob and Claude had a very unique, at least unique at the time, way of thinking about the overall portfolio. At the same time, the plan was included in the Ontario Province's non-marketable bond portfolio. So one of the first things that Bob and Claude did, which was quite innovative at the time, was to use financial engineering and a derivatives program to turn these non-marketable bonds into a liquid portfolio of global public equities. And that was the first step towards diversification across a number of different asset classes. We were one of the first to use private equity, infrastructure, commodities, hedge funds, etc. And then, 35 years later, we have a $300 million plan. We cover the pension benefits of 346,000 active retired teachers in the province. We have a global presence with offices in North America, Europe and Asia. And we have real experience in direct internal implementation of asset management. Ultimately, this resulted in a funding ratio of 111%, which really helps with the long-term sustainability of the plan. So, throughout all of this experience, public markets, private markets, TFM positions, and today you hold the position of Co-Chief Information Technology Officer. How would you describe the current strategy at OTPP? Well, ultimately, we're trying to build a diversified portfolio that's resilient across different economic environments to really ensure that we can deliver on that retirement promise across different environments. And so there are a few levers you can pull to achieve this. And I would divide such an investment strategy along several different dimensions. One of which would be diversification. And how do you get this diversification? First, we believe in active management, so it's where and how you focus your activities to get that excess return. Another aspect is where you focus on ensuring the right risk management system is in place to achieve this ultimate goal. And the fourth aspect is that we use a reasonable amount of leverage to implement and execute our investment plan . So, those are four directions. How do you feel about implementing, uh, TPA or DFM? TPA is an interesting topic, and I think a lot of institutions probably have a variant or form of this in terms of how they think about a portfolio, because at the end of the day, the key is to create the best risk-adjusted portfolio with all the tools at your disposal. I think our form of this probably started with a TPA type back in 2015 or 2016, when we went down the path of a single- teacher strategy, where our board of directors would ask management, " Okay, what's the desired asset mix?" Management represented the board of directors. The board of directors said, " Okay, great, this is the right asset mix." Management then tried to create a portfolio that would outperform such an asset mix, and that this asset mix would have some of the characteristics of a risky portfolio. And one of the challenges is making sure that there is alignment with what you are actually trying to do, and that pensions are paid out with total returns, not just active returns or just beta returns. So how do you make sure you are in a situation where everyone is aligned to deliver the best overall risk-adjusted return? And so, when we were looking at one teacher's strategy, the board of directors said, " Hey, look, we're signing this asset inventory, but this is what you're recommending to us. Why are we taking responsibility for this? Is there a way for you to be responsible for the asset inventory as much as we are?" And that really put us on the path to creating much more flexible ranges of asset allocations. The flip side of that is that it doesn't mean you don't have a rigorous approach to risk, but what we do have , and I think that's one of the extensions of that discussion, and I've had conversations with people who have been on this podcast, other colleagues in the US, etc. about this concept of a benchmark portfolio, and for me, a benchmark portfolio is more of a signal of risk appetite, not necessarily meant to give you a rigorous portfolio construction exercise. And so I always say, " Look, if you're going to tell me what the right risk appetite is, just tell me directly." And then it's up to the management and the investment team to ensure the best risk-adjusted return to achieve that, consistent with all the precautions that you would have in place from a risk perspective. And I think some of the downsides of having a benchmark portfolio is that over time, I would argue, investment teams will gravitate toward those weights, and you might find yourself in a situation where, for example, your benchmark portfolio is 60% equities , 40% fixed income, our investment teams will be very reluctant to deviate significantly from those weights. And so you may find yourself in a world where you have a large exposure to fixed income, as we saw in 2020, 2021 , where the reason for it in the portfolio may not be as compelling as it once was; and so you end up in a situation where investment teams are very reluctant to deviate, even though they know they have to . How do you put all of this together, and is it some form of TPA overall fund management structure? How does it all fit together? This is really a central element of how the overall management of the fund functions. And it's more than just that, because, again , the overall management of the fund is really focused on the top-down asset allocation function. And how do you then layer it "bottom up" thinking like that? And this is where the real magic happens in terms of excess returns. So I'll start with maybe some of the levers that we use top-down, and then we can maybe move on to some bottom-up. So, top-down is more my area of expertise, and my colleague Gillian will be responsible for that bottom-up, but top-down, some of the levers that we would have would be your combination of active and passive? What is your formulation of leverage and liquidity, if you will, to implement this overall asset mix? I think the main thing that the team spends a lot of time on is where and how do you want to position the portfolio from a broader risk perspective? And, you know, it can be very complicated, and we have a lot of different systems that really take that into account; but our simpler way of thinking is whether we want the portfolio to be positioned aggressively, neutrally or conservatively, depending on the market environment , and really overlaying our risk/return ratios to meet our actuarial objectives. As you know, we are a pension plan, so we have a pretty good overview in terms of our liability profile, even though it could be 60, 70, 80 years. So looking today and just thinking about this high level, do you want to be aggressively neutral or conservative, how do you make that assessment? Of course. Well, we have several different processes or planning horizons, and frankly, investment committees for that. So the first one is our investment planning process, which is perhaps typical for the industry, but we develop an annual investment plan where we try to think about what we want the portfolio to look like in one year. We also think about the planning process over a five-year horizon. And, listen, five years—there's nothing magical about it. It's far enough in the future that you don't need to do anything immediately today, but it's close enough that you actually have to start taking action today if you want to achieve it. And the five-year horizon is actually driven by the fact that we have a portion of the portfolio that is in illiquid assets, so we need to make sure that we have the right buffer to be able to manage that because you never want to be in a position where you are forced to sell an asset. And so we spend a lot of time planning where we think those distributions should go, and we also combine that with a fairly significant and rigorous liquidity and leverage framework that is managed by our risk management team. This one-year horizon process, which is probably more about the risk positioning aspect because you maybe need to have a little more visibility into one year, although it's very complex, is really the beginning of how we want to structure the portfolio. Given this, a one-year horizon is still an eternity in the investment business. And so there's a function within our fund management team that looks at more dynamic types of opportunities and how the market might evolve, and how does that compare to our initial assumptions? And that doesn't mean they are high-frequency traders. And I want to say that the point of TFM is not to day trade a portfolio. These are important decisions, and frankly, we have a group that has a specific mandate within our capital markets management team that will be much more frequent in nature. But the TFM team and this dynamic team are really here to say, " Look, here's what we think is in the situation." Here's what, in our opinion, is currently included or not included in the market price. And then how should we look at portfolio adjustments , which are actually driven by a number of things. One of them would be an approach aimed at reducing risks. So if there is a certain event on the horizon that, if it were to occur, would simply be unacceptable from a profitability or catastrophic loss perspective, we probably want to think about it. A prototypical example of this would be , you know, Brexit 10 years ago: if you have a large portfolio of UK bonds or sterling and you just don't know what's going to happen, maybe you should think about trying to manage some of that risk more aggressively . So, that would be an example of this particular part. Another example: “Hey, look, we have an allocation in the portfolio. Markets have changed. Will it still serve its role in the portfolio given the revaluation that has occurred?” “And an example of that would be 2022, for example, with fixed income. We had a fixed income allocation because we follow that all-weather philosophy. And when yields continued to fall lower and lower to almost zero, so that would be from 2020 to 2022, sorry. We did a lot of analysis, and our CIO at the time, working with our CEO and board of directors, took some time and said, “ Hey, look, our expected return for fixed income is pretty low because the return was close to zero .” I fully understand that yields could turn negative, as has happened and is happening in Europe, but we believe that is less likely to happen in North America, given some of the comments from central banks and other authorities in North America. So the role of fixed income in a portfolio as a compensation or ballast for an equity shock will be more complex. "So why do we have this in our briefcase?" And so it was probably a very good decision, given what happened to the fixed income markets after that, but at the same time a very conscious decision to reduce our fixed income exposure. And that would be driven by a combination of discussions and research on the part of this TFM group. So I would like you to tell us, let's say, about your last year's process. What are your thoughts on the five-year and one-year periods ? I think five years is also long enough to make sure you have enough flexibility because a lot can change. But we spent a lot of time thinking about what we need to focus our activities on? And how do we want to position the portfolio for that? So, you know, a typical example of this is private equity. And what is the expected return for private equity? Um, you know, some of our colleagues in the US, for example, have been much more aggressive in reducing what they consider to be the expected return on these assets. We believe that private equity has become more competitive in terms of what that expected return will be. So, if you've previously earned or projected to earn, I don't know, five or six hundred basis points more than your benchmark, if it's less, then you probably want to think about what the implications of that are going to be for the portfolio over that five-year horizon. But you never want to be in a situation where you're, so to speak , closing the door, and if market conditions change, and I think there's a good chance that those market conditions are changing, you won't be able to execute. Because we use the services of partners, but we also have a team of internal investors who can also implement these measures. Therefore, managing this aspect is a fairly important piece of the puzzle. So when you want to bend a little bit, let's say, reduce the share of private equity a little bit in that scenario, how do you do that? You need to start thinking about who you want to be and how you envision the team in place. And, listen, sometimes you need to have patience so you don't do something reckless or chaotic. We have the advantage of being fully funded and having a very flexible liquidity pool, so we never find ourselves in a situation where we need to hit a certain level. So we have taken an approach where we should look for opportunities to reduce this when we believe the market or pricing for these assets is attractive and still consistent with our long-term profitability assumptions, but not overly push this allocation. So in that scenario, where you were thinking over the course of 5 years that you might want to scale back from where you were, how do you switch external connections to internal capabilities? I think part of it is also due to the reduction in the dollar size of this program , probably not as noticeable as you think, as the fund will continue to grow. And that gives you some leverage to support the asset allocation function, which is trying to allocate them on a percentage basis as we try to scale the overall portfolio. But as you know, if you're a practicing physician, a family doctor, or an in-house investor, you're also focused on how many dollars I have. And it actually provided some kind of compensator for what could have been much more draconian circumstances. So we didn't actually see a significant decrease in the dollar amount because when we forecast these things, it kind of offset that percentage decrease. When you went from your five-year perspective to your one-year perspective, what things do you think have changed in the one-year perspective? Well, recently, I think there's been a lot of discussion and thought about our inflation- sensitive asset class , which is a little different from maybe some of our competitors. And as I mentioned in previous parts, we are advocates of this kind of all-weather or sustainable portfolio creation. And our inflation-sensitive asset class, which we currently have about 20% of the portfolio in, really exists for two purposes. One is to provide reasonable returns in most environments, but certainly in a spike in inflation or a more inflationary environment, which has historically been the case and , in our estimation, will have a rather negative impact on equity and bond portfolios in the future. So in those cases, our inflation-sensitive asset class really exists to offset what we expect in our stock market. And in this basket we have several levers. Our inflation sensitives will be our government goods, which I talked about earlier, including gold. We have a private natural resources team that I grew up with in the organization, so I'm familiar with it. And it also has a whole suite of inflation-linked products on the public market to provide us with that protection. So we spent a lot of time thinking about what this inflationary environment would look like? How do we need to position this part of the portfolio in a world where we expect more inflation volatility and probably more weight. So this is one area that we spent a lot of time on. Another thing about the basket of stocks in terms of how you envision the composition of your stocks? We have private equity, we have venture capital , we have the public or passive portion of the portfolio, and there are both positive and negative aspects to each of these dimensions. On the passive side, obviously, concentration in the US is something we are thinking about or trying to think about in terms of how you manage it. And you know, the reality is that the US is still a pretty important market, and if you really want to have access to the AI ​​development topic , it's hard to find it in other markets, so we need to be thoughtful about how we properly shape or build that part of the portfolio, but we spend a lot of time thinking about some of these issues that lie beneath the surface. When you look at this one factor of AI and growth through the lens of risk, there's a lot of discussion about this potential binary outcome where it just keeps going , and they keep winning, or maybe something changes significantly. How do you factor this into your thinking about portfolio risk? I think AI is changing so quickly that it's very difficult to have a clear vision and conviction , so we try to be humble about the fact that there are certain things we don't know, and you can debate whether other people know, but certainly we want to be balanced in terms of approach and not be too confident in our ability to predict what or how this AI topic will develop. I think the other part is that we want to make sure that we look at the portfolio from this all-weather perspective and that we don't over-hype, if you will, on a particular outcome related to AI. This is even more important given the range of outcomes associated with it, which makes it even more important to think about the sustainability of this portfolio, recognizing that there are benefits associated with it, but there are also potential drawbacks to what you're hinting at. For example, what happens if AI turns upside down? Given this, if AI turns out to be a very positive productivity shock, then historically it has actually benefited the equity part of the capital structure. So how do you make sure you take into account all the different economic scenarios? What are some of the recent dynamic shifts you've made in this year's basket, probably on the liquidity side? I don't want to get too deep into specific tactics, but I mentioned some of the work we've been doing on inflation-sensitive issues. And, obviously, there was a lot of volatility in the commodity markets . So we used that as an opportunity where it was appropriate and where it was related to how we think about the impact on other asset classes. So, if there is an inflationary shock, how much of that inflationary shock have you already factored in in terms of some of these baskets? So we spend a lot of time on it. How do you feel about liquidity? And you mentioned using some leverage, and those two things can combine across the entire portfolio. So, I would divide it into a kind of triangle: leverage, liquidity, and funding. And I will try to consider it as a whole. This is managed by our treasury team. And our risk management team also has a pretty substantial process that helps us manage that part of the portfolio. You know, I think leverage and liquidity are very important because what could get any investor into trouble? And by trouble, I mean they're going to be pushed out of their belief in how they think a portfolio should be structured , which is, first of all , you have a liquidity event and you can't meet your short-term obligations. And that's one thing. Secondly, you lose a lot of money. So how do you make sure you don't lose a lot of money? And third, are you doing things that your stakeholders don't like , and how do you make sure you manage that? Regarding liquidity, this is particularly important given that we use derivatives to build our portfolio, so we have a very rigorous process of scenario and stress analysis to ensure that we have consistently strong liquidity. This is actually a board of directors restriction for us. We have a certain process, so we spend a lot of time monitoring that. I think there have been a few instances, both in the US where some funds have gone through the World Finance Corporation and even in the Canadian pension space, where some of these credit positions that didn't have a core comprehensive liquidity management profile have led to problems for some institutions where they have had to sell assets at very inopportune times, and we certainly want to avoid those circumstances. What metrics do you use to calibrate the appropriate amount of liquidity? We would use a liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) type indicator as an integral part of this process. This is not exactly the same as what you would see at a bank or a depository institution, as our liability structure is significantly different from a depository, but it is very similar to the LCR ratio set up for a pension plan. What is convenient for you? It's convenient for me to be able to absorb a fairly significant shock and again not be pushed out of position. And this depends on the size of the portfolio, and also has implications, for example, for currency hedging . You, as a US investor, may have a slightly different problem with currencies where you tend to hedge an illiquid long-term asset with a liquid security and therefore you have some liquidity or maturity mismatch. And what usually happens during a market shock is that the U.S. dollar, in this case, strengthens relative to the Canadian dollar. If you were doing any hedging, you typically have to provide collateral for that, and that would be one of the sources of liquidity that we think about a lot , and that would be factored into our LCR system. Have you thought about where to implement active management and where to simply receive passive influence? It all comes down to where you think you have an advantage, and where you can achieve it while having the ability to generate excess income. And this can be done both internally and externally. So it's broader than just, " Hey, look, you should just do infrastructure with external or internal managers." I think it comes down to what we talked about earlier, about what the necessary ingredients are for a particular strategy to be able to deliver excess income. And what have been the driving forces historically, and what do you think those driving forces will be in the future? And then use that to say, as I said before, what is active versus passive negotiation, which is more of a top-down versus bottom- up solution, where the bottom-up deal teams are going to have to say, "Hey, look, this is where I think we can add value, and this is where we're going to focus our efforts to get those results." So, looking at asset classes, where have you decided to use active management? For example, active vs. passive in one case, and then internal vs. external in another, if you fill it out twice. I think recently we've really come to a conclusion or really positioned the portfolio in the equity space by saying, " Listen, passive equity versus an active public equity program has been much more challenging, at least for us." I know there are some institutions, so we have cut this program. We have a team that is still actively picking stocks, but it is smaller than it was a few years ago, given the fact that it is a very complex and competitive market, and how do we want to think about allocating our resources? I think when we look at other asset classes, private equity, infrastructure and real estate are the big three, as well as venture capital, and so maybe we can spend a few minutes on venture capital because it creates another level of complexity. To the extent that these opportunities are successful, we really use a hybrid model of external and internal, depending on where the market is and where we think we have some competitive advantage , to be able to deliver that excess profitability. But we really try to be thoughtful about where we focus our internal resources.” and where, again, coming back to this moment of humility, where we just need to acknowledge that it is in an area of ​​expertise or activity that we are best placed to work with an external partner. What do you think about using hedge funds in your portfolio? So, I think hedge funds, at least on paper, from a top-down perspective, fall into what we call our absolute return strategies, and the theoretical part of that is that they have high expected returns with low correlation to some of the other underlying assets that we have. These are stocks and bonds. They are very hard to find, and when you can find them, you need to think carefully about what or how you factor in the commission component , so we spend a lot of time on that. We use hedge funds in that capacity to generate uncorrelated returns, but also in certain cases where there's a certain skill set or a certain type of income stream that these people can provide and we just can't do it internally. We are open to using this as leverage to implement into our asset mix. How did you view the internal use of hedge funds? We have a capital markets team that does hedge fund-like strategies. One example is that we have a quantitative systematic research team, so they use some of the same methods that you see in some of the big hedge funds, but they do it internally. You mentioned venture capital and growth. How do you implement it from this side? I think our venture team, or what we call TVG, which stands for Teacher Venture Growth, was formed in 2019. It played a role in the portfolio at the time, giving us access to innovative companies that weren't necessarily available on the public market. This team did a fantastic job. One of the key stages, as you know, for a venture capital company is its public listing . This is a rather important event, which overall represents a truly excellent result. I would say that a venture capital company going public is a feature, not a mistake, but from a portfolio perspective it creates this tension between private and public investing. So we have to think more and more often... about this. That's not to say that such cases haven't happened in the past with our private equity team or INR, but it wasn't as big of a problem. And I think we tried to be practical, given the difference in mindset between a private and a public investor , given the fact that the TVG team would have the most knowledge about these particular organizations. And as these companies that have now gone through an IPO become more mature, you probably need to start thinking about how best to position them in terms of a more private or, sorry, more public context , but for now, we've decided that we want the people with the best information to be closest to this asset, and for those individuals to be the most responsible for it. So for now we're keeping them in the TVG group . How have you been thinking about the position size of something as we get some of these massive IPOs that you didn't have control over and now you do? Again, I would say these are world- class problems when you have an asset that has become like 10, 20, 30, 40 beggars or whatever. So this is a different form of problem in terms of the concentration risk that you have grown into, as opposed to another problem related to just a large position. With that in mind, we want to make sure we are thoughtful and aware of the risks. So for some of these concentrated positions, we want to make sure that we're not overly concentrated, and to the extent that market circumstances allow, regardless of how attractive these entities may be or what the prospects for these companies may be, we have lines of risk. And so we want to make sure that we don't have an over- concentration on one name in the portfolio. How did you approach some of your historical directions , credit, infrastructure and resource portions of the portfolios? Lending is definitely interesting from a top- down perspective, and look, I grew up in the lending business here, so I have a lot of affection for the team there, and I think that plays a role in the portfolio . It has a great...kind of cash yield, can have a great spike rate or information rate, and certainly has a form of risk premium that you could call volatility or some volatility-related impact factor. I think that as I've moved to a more top-down approach, I fully understand that it plays a role in generating alpha, but I always struggle with the notion of credit where from a portfolio construction perspective , when you want it to act like an equity, it acts like a fixed income. And I mean, when it's a really positive growth environment , and stocks are really showing big gains, by design you're limited. I think the other downside of credit or the other problem with credit is that when you want it to act like fixed income, it acts like an equity. So how do you think about building a portfolio, recognizing that it plays a role, but it also has these other characteristics that depending on how extreme the overall macro environment is, you might end up with something that you don't need or want in the portfolio. So what you described regarding credit is kind of a negative skew for lack of a better way to say it. How to do it? You take that lens and decide something that you know a lot about , decide how you want to implement it in the portfolio? I think we're very fortunate that we have a very broad range of activities in the fund, so any program is really part of a larger portfolio, so that's how we would think about it . What, what or how does this particular asset affect, how is it affected by, and how does it contribute to the overall portfolio? You know, by the way, another observation I've had is that diversification is a very powerful portfolio tool, but at any given time it's likely to make you unhappy, and people say, "What are you talking about?" And I give the example of most investment committees, and even when I do a portfolio review with the team, we look at the line of all asset classes or all securities, and then we gravitate to the things that are above the line and say, "Hey, look, this is really great." "Things down the line, people's natural reaction will be, ' Why are we doing this?'" "And I think that's a good question, but I think you need to look at the context of the expected contribution of these things above and below the line, and how do they interact? And that's another way to express that diversification. So when we think about the overall portfolio, I always keep in mind how we think each of these components is going to contribute to our overall objective, which is obviously to deliver risk-adjusted returns. How do you combine that with the risk reward that you mentioned in credit, where it's not performing as well as you would like in different environments? That's how we look at it and say let's use a fairly simple growth versus inflation metric, and you can start to think about what kind of environment are you projecting? And credit does well in a low volatility environment, and other asset classes may not do as well. So it's more of a holistic approach to that, and so I'm somewhat torn with certain from an asset allocation perspective, because in a large slice or a large set of results it will work quite well. So how do you imagine these so-called tail results? I'm using a rather generous term for tails, but how do you imagine these particular states of the world, and what other parts of the portfolio do you need to compensate for what might be happening for this particular asset class? So one of those compensations would be infrastructure. I'd love to hear how you approached implementing the infrastructure part. We've been doing infrastructure directly since 2002-2003. So we were very early adopters of that asset class. I think infrastructure has some very interesting characteristics, and it's roughly in line with our overall risk profile. And I mean you can add infrastructure and it won't be too out of sync with what I think our desired risk profile is. So that's been a big contributor to the overall fund. over the last 20-plus years. And our implementation has been to do it directly with the team. Um, these assets tend to be much more scalable than what you might see in some of the other regions. So we have a team not only here in North America but also in Europe and Asia that is really looking at these opportunities. And it really provides cash flow stability and real rate exposure, which is quite attractive when we think about the overall portfolio. When you're planning how the infrastructure is going to work in a number of these states of the world. If you look at the entire portfolio, what is the proportion of your internally managed assets versus externally managed assets? There's no pre- set number. I think we just need to be careful about saying, " Hey, this has to be a certain number." "I think we're trying to be thoughtful and pragmatic that in certain cases, partners, in this case, GPs, because partners can mean portfolio companies that we invest in and other forms of that. But in this particular context, I would single out the type of GP. Are we getting , um, good value for money ? And in many cases we get. So it depends on the market. It depends on how we think our own internal capabilities will be able to deliver what we think is the appropriate risk-reward ratio. So there are no pre- set rules as such. Um, but we would like to be thoughtful and flexible and not be in a situation where you have to give a specific number because I think that leads to overflowing the bucket, which can never be a good thing. What is the range of the proportion of external managers that you have had over time? I don't know what the exact numbers will be, but I would say it will be anywhere, depending on the program. So each group will have a different distribution and it also depends on the... " maturity level. But, I would say the ratio ranges from 10 to 30%, it will be external to some extent , and it also depends on the activity. And when you look for an external manager, what does that process look like? We have specialized teams both from a private equity perspective and from a non-private equity perspective. groups that are really focused on these fund relationships. So they'll go through, you know, a more typical kind of origination funnel around what, what or where we're trying to focus our expertise or exposure. So they'll go through a market screening and think about what the environment is in whatever sector or geography that we're talking about and then go out and meet with partners and then start thinking about what the appropriate way to allocate capital is, uh, in terms of advancing that part of the business. What are some of the common characteristics of partners that you gravitate towards? I think first and foremost, is having a partner that wants us to be their partner. I think that's pretty important in terms of them being able to realize that we can be not just an equity partner but also be an input into how they think about the different businesses that they're taking on. That would be one of them. Um, we also ultimately want to make sure that we get the required return and productivity for the commissions paid. I would like to talk about the structure of your team. And maybe let's start at the top, with this dual CIO structure , which you don't hear about very often. You mentioned the different roles. How do you come together to make decisions? Just for the record, as you mentioned, we have a dual role of CIO or co- CIO, and that was actually after, as I explained earlier, the resignation of the previous CIO. And we took that as an opportunity to think about what would be best for the future, given that the world has become much more complex. The fund has grown significantly over the last 35 years. And the number of asset classes has increased, the number of investors that are part of the investment group has increased. quite significantly, and the world has become much more complex. And so we made the decision or the decision to move to a dual CIO model, but we clearly understand that each of us has our own area of expertise, if you will, or our own responsibilities. I I would explain it this way. I'm responsible for asset allocation, and we've been discussing this for a while. My colleague, Gillian Brown, is responsible for the public and private investment function. We've been working together for quite a while, so we know each other very well as individuals. But where we have a more formal intersection, other than how you oversee the overall portfolio, is that the regional offices report to me, and one of the main goals of our regional offices is to deliver active returns. So there's a natural connection or a natural intersection between how we need to oversee the business. A simple example to explain how we use this in practice is that we have two main investment committees. We have the overall fund investment committee, which is more of one of those broader asset allocation functions, stocks, bonds, commodities, etc. And I chair that. Gillian is a member of that committee, so she'll be able to give me some context either in the meeting or outside of it. And then we have another investment committee called the public and private investment committee , and she chairs it. I 'm a member of that, and it's actually responsible for overseeing our large public and private investments. So those are the more formal structural parts of the fund. I think the other things that we use to make sure that we're managing the portfolio effectively are weekly meetings with our CEO and our CFO , where any of these extreme questions or decisions that are probably closer to being used, using the concept of economic indifference, where there 's not necessarily a right answer, but, you know, there's some need for debate and discussion. We have regular meetings with our CEO and our CFO . The other part of it is just making sure that we're constantly communicating with each other, and ultimately it comes down to... a level of trust and, frankly, respect for each other's areas of expertise, so that we don't run into serious conflict when we try to make some of these key decisions. And I think if there was a serious problem, which there wasn't for the reasons I just mentioned, we would ultimately look to our CEO to help us resolve it through arbitration or adjudication, but to date that hasn't been an issue. What's an example of some of the most interesting conversations you've had on one or both of the investment committees recently? There's been a number of transactions that we've looked at in the private sector, in a number of sectors where we're trying to be thoughtful: "Okay, look, what's the risk of failure for these businesses?" and "And again, on the previous conversations that we've had about AI in general, it's very difficult to have high conviction. So we're in the investment business and it's an inherent part of making decisions under uncertainty, but there's been a lot of discussion and debate on that side. And then at the general fund level, you know, lately it's really been about the overall risk positioning and in terms of what we want it to be, neutral, conservative, aggressive, etc., and how we manage that particular piece. So as expected, I would say, but on the right questions that these groups should be talking about. When you look at it today, through the lens of conservative, neutral, aggressive, how do you view the world? It's a complex world, and, you know, I would say it fluctuates from period to period, but I think we probably hold the view that we're probably best positioned a little bit more in that neutral range. And again , the challenge is that it can change, but we try to be quite thoughtful and have a serious debate about where or how we should think about the overall portfolio positioning. And then, as we have a number of different instruments, how do we modulate or how do we adjust these types of exposures? If you look at history, how often have you been in that neutral category versus one end? Most of the time you're probably in the neutral category, just given the fact that markets are pretty good at pricing, and that doesn't mean they're exceptionally efficient. I think that, uh, my observation is that market efficiency on average is that they're efficient, and there are always pockets where things are overpriced and other areas where they're underpriced, but generally the starting point is that they're probably fairly priced. So then you need to be quite selective. How do your internal and external investment teams communicate and work together? I I think that's something that we've spent a lot of time on over the last 10 or 15 years to ensure that there's a good flow of information. these two groups. And in some cases, uh, they're more integrated and part of the teams more directly. But certainly that's something that you need to focus on in terms of having a regular dialogue between these interns, these internal people, and also making sure that there's a good connection between , uh, the direct teams and these funds. In what areas have you found more synergy between the internal and external teams ? Certainly in some of the hedge fund areas, and so we have some of the big public market strategies where, uh, the partners in those areas are real employees and have great, so to speak, intellectual property or great dialogue with our internal teams in terms of issues that we might have with structuring a certain part of the portfolio, how we think about some of these other aspects that we talked about, liquidity, etc. How do you use things like artificial intelligence, to enhance the portfolio? Uh , so some of those things, and so there's been a really great collaboration that I could specifically mention, certainly in those areas. You mentioned the regional offices that report to you. I'm curious what those offices do. Just for reference, our regional offices have a team in Europe that covers, uh , a number of sectors. That includes infrastructure. We have a venture capital group there. We have, uh, real estate investors there, and we have private equity investors there, and also, uh, in Asia we have a team in Singapore and also a team in Mumbai. And those areas of activity are more focused on, uh, infrastructure, private equity and venture capital. And those teams, as I said, are really tasked with providing the fund with potential impact. Again, we don't have a forced geographic allocation , but we have to be opportunistic and make sure that we really we use this diversification lever. So those teams are really tasked with going out and finding, looking for and managing the assets to create value in those respective markets in those respective asset classes. What did you think about the reporting lines of the people on the ground looking at the assets versus, uh, Julian? I think we use, uh, and we work in a matrix model that requires both an asset class and a regional head who has to support the deal. It's really to make sure that we're combining what's good for the overall portfolio with what the local knowledge that the deal teams in those regions actually have to bring. And that's been the method that we've used so far , and we expect to use it going forward. I wanted to ask you about the evolution of the Canadian model over the 20-plus years that you've been at Teachers. What do you think the competitive advantages of the model have remained? I would start with what the Canadian model is or what its key characteristics? And I think those would be some of the main ones, and I think it's broader than just governance or governance independence. It would be diversification, and it would be different degrees of internal governance. And so I think that would really be a kind of training. And then, for context, I think 20 or 25 years ago there just weren't a lot of people who had those characteristics and had enough capital to be able to... actually do these specific things. I think if you go to today, you 'll see a lot more organizations that have a similar set of characteristics. So the competition or the uniqueness of where we were 20 years ago is significantly different. And that's something we need to think about . Where are we now or how does this Canadian model compare? I would say that, um, the advantage is that we have a long-term horizon. It may not be like another pension plan, but it's a difference compared to a GP or another an organization that might have a fixed term and has to do certain things with its portfolio. Um, of course, we have a long history of good partnerships and the ability to deliver and fulfill everything that we promise. I think the third point that positions us quite well is that we have institutional memory, and you can say, " What does this mean?" ""I think we have all the processes, the board management, we have the back office, the deal-making unions that everyone can do. Sometimes it's taken for granted, and of course when I talk to some of my colleagues in the U.S. and certainly in other parts of the world, they say, 'Oh my God, you need to build all this infrastructure and so on.'" We already have that. Another advantage is that we have one cohort of beneficiaries, and that allows us to create one portfolio that is completely aligned with the whole group. And there's a real affinity with our mission. So most people have had a really positive experience with a teacher in their lives. There's a natural affinity to that, and it's a great way to not only attract partners, but also have staff that can recruit and retain staff. So it all ties them together. I think the biggest advantage, at least for us, and I think for the Canadian group of colleagues in general, is that we are generally very well funded, and in our case we have a funding ratio of…111%. You might say, “Well , big deal, what does that mean?” And what that really means is that we can choose where on the risk curve we want to play. And people get into trouble, or investors get into trouble, when they're forced into a risky position that they're not comfortable with, and that's when mistakes happen. We can be the masters of our own destiny and actually choose where on the risk curve we want to play based on where we think the best market opportunities are. Given this fully funded status, how do you feel about the goals of continuing to grow the pool versus just maintaining a fully funded status? That's a really good question . I think where we are right now, we're not at a point where we can maybe make a more informed decision. Well, it's not really my, uh, my decision. It's up to the sponsors, so I don't want to overstep, like, my, uh, my role on that particular point. But we spend a lot of time thinking about where you, uh, optimally risked? So, how do you think about that given the change in the funding ratio? And where we are now, we're not at that point, and that allows us to focus on what our, I would say, actuarial yield is and make sure that we execute on that to ensure, uh, pension solvency or pension payments over the long term . And where does that show up in the numbers? Our stated goal, again, on a, uh, risk-adjusted basis, is to deliver a 7% nominal yield, uh, on a perpetual basis. What are some of the ways that the early advantages of the Canadian model no longer exist? I think the ability to write a big check and get preferential terms on a deal with whoever is selling them is certainly gone. I think there's just been a broader increase in competition for a lot of these assets, so more competition means a compression of the expected yield. And that's not necessarily unique to Canadian model, but I think it's a phenomenon that we're seeing across all markets because there's just more capital coming in, and the ability of...that capital to have some access to what you might call private equity returns or alternative returns is just a compressed excess return premium. How do you assess the strengths and in some cases the weaknesses of your size? I think the strength of our size really gives us room to do different things, so we're not forced to do one particular set of activities. I think it also helps retail attract and retain staff because it allows you to say, "Hey, look, do you want to be a really good investor and hone all your skills throughout the investment lifecycle?" And that would include origination , asset management , execution, and also different asset classes. Look, I'm a prime example. I've done a lot of different things internally, publicly, privately, combining all of that together. So I think the size of the business, the scale and the scope of the business really helps that aspect both from a people perspective and a portfolio perspective. What are some of the investment themes that you're most excited about? I think when you think about how the world has changed since COVID, let's just use that... as a point of demarcation. What are some of the major themes? One of them is the increased cost of capital, and that could be related to higher inflation, but it could also be related to other reasons, and just higher risk-free rates, which generally translate into higher required returns across a number of different asset classes. And that's one of the things that we've spent a lot of time thinking about. I think the second one is related to geopolitics and how that will evolve, and it used to be mostly focused on the US- China relationship in terms of how these two great powers were going to think and evolve over the next 5, 10, 15, 20 years. It's become a little bit broader lately. And then the third category is technology and, in particular, artificial intelligence recently. But those are the three main things that we're trying to just think about: How is this going to affect our overall portfolio? How is this going to affect the growth profile? How is this going to affect the inflation portfolio ? How do we need to adjust now to make sure that we're still in a position to have a sound portfolio, recognizing that we think the future states of the world or the range of outcomes have expanded significantly over the last few years. If you look at your five-year projections, taking into account the cost of capital, geopolitics and technology, how do you try to adjust the portfolio to be best positioned for these changes? On each of those, honestly, I think we trying to approach it with a certain amount of modesty and say, “Look, what’s the general direction of the impact on growth and inflation?” “And how is that going to interact with different parts of the portfolio? I don’t know if there are any specific areas that I would like to comment on.” Hey, we think that AI is going to have a giant productivity shock, and that’s going to be really good for asset prices in general . “I would hesitate to be immodest or overconfident in making those kinds of predictions. So I think we’re trying to be a little bit more simple about things and say, “Look, we don’t have high convictions on a lot of these points. So let’s make sure that we’re running a balanced portfolio and that we have the right set of scenarios so that we don’t end up in a big drawdown situation.” What are the most important initiatives from Teachers over the next few years? I think the main one , at least for me, is to ensure that we have a good understanding of how "We're using AI as a business, in terms of providing the right tools for people and ultimately using those technologies to make better decisions. I think that's where the real prize lies. Obviously it's productivity gains, and how can you make sure that people are the most productive or the most effective ?" But for me, it's: How do you make sure that you're leveraging access to all of this information, and how can AI analyze and manipulate that information to make better decisions in terms of how we factor that into our own investment decision-making process ? Great. So, Stephen, I want to make sure that I have a chance to ask you a few final questions. What's the most rewarding thing for you outside of work? I enjoy being the CIO of this institution and the wealth manager for 346,000 teachers in Ontario, but it's quite a lot of work. So spending time with friends and family is pretty important, and of course in the winter I love to snowboard, but in the summer it's really time because we're very lucky to have a cottage, but we're very lucky to have time there, spending time outdoors, fishing, etc. What was your first paid job and what did you learn from it ? In high school I had typical retail jobs , lifeguard, etc., but my first paid job was delivering newspapers for the Ottawa Citizen. And you know, again, a couple of life skills, you know, having to show up every day to get paid, even though it probably only took 30 minutes or so. But as a tie-in to my experience in lending, another aspect of being a newspaper carrier was collecting accounts receivable, because after you delivered the newspapers you had to go back and collect every few weeks for $3 or whatever it was. And strangely, there were always a few houses where no one was home, even though you could see the TV was on. So that was a lot of fun and a real lesson. What are the two people who have had the biggest impact on your professional life? When I look back on the last 30 years of my career, I would focus on a couple of things. One of them would be my experience as an investment banker in Calgary. One of my bosses at the time was Chris Burley. Chris was incredibly smart, incredibly hardworking, but he had a real knack that I still try to emulate, preparing for any meetings, sessions , negotiations, etc. And he really used that, at least from my perspective, as a very useful exercise, a kind of game theory or war game , to understand what the other side might be thinking. And I think that was a very useful and informative part of my career. The other aspect is that I've been very lucky. I've worked for every CEO and every CIO of Teachers since it was founded. So each one of them has added something to me and impressed me over that period of time. But maybe I suffer or succumb to a newness bias, which I know I shouldn't. I'd like to thank Joe Taylor, our CEO, and Gillian Brown, my co-CIO, who really provided a support network not only from an investment perspective side, but also some of the broader issues around running the business, people and other constraints that we need, or other aspects of the overall puzzle of running a business. And I think honorable mention would be Ziad Hindo, who was the previous CIO , who was a great investor and a big influence on me . But I think one of the things he always said, and that still sticks with me, is that you have to do what you think is right for the portfolio, even if some people disagree with you . You have to believe in what you're doing, and that's stuck in my mind, and that's certainly something I've tried to keep in mind when I think about the portfolio now. Okay, Stephen, one last thing. What's a life lesson you've learned that you wish you had learned earlier in your life? Earlier in my career, I had a lot of this kind of fear of missing out, like, "Listen, why did this person get this opportunity, this job, this promotion?" And one piece of advice that I got, and I wish I had known it before, was, "Listen, be mindful and think about what you think the next stage of your career is going to be, or what role you want to have next." And it could be getting more technical knowledge, it could be developing your leadership skills, or something else; and just be mindful of what that might be. And then when other opportunities come up , don't get too worked up if that particular role doesn't fit that opportunity. And I think if you look at it that way and say, "Look, my colleague just got this particular role," and you might think, "Oh my God, I wish I had that," and then you think and say, "Well, I don't even want to do that, so why am I mumbling about it?" Stephen, thank you so much for sharing this wonderful review of teachers. Great, no, thank you for inviting me. Mmm.
